parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by a photon.
hints: Hint 1: Think about whether light energy arrives continuously like water from a tap, or in tiny discrete lumps.
Hint 2: Remember what kind of radiation light is, and link the lump of energy to that radiation.
parts.proper_answer: A photon is a discrete packet (quantum) of energy of electromagnetic radiation.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Quantised Means**
Think of light as being able to behave as a wave but also as a stream of particles. You cannot have half a particle, so the energy cannot be split continuously. It comes in tiny indivisible lumps.

Step 2: **Complete Definition**
That lump is called a photon. So you say: $$E = hf$$ is the energy of one photon, where a photon is a packet or quantum of energy of electromagnetic radiation.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Light in a beam has a continuous spectrum that lies within the visible region. The photons of light have energies ranging from $1.60\text{ eV}$ to $2.60\text{ eV}$.

The beam passes through some hydrogen gas. It then passes through a diffraction grating and an absorption spectrum is observed.
parts.text: All of the light absorbed by the hydrogen is re-emitted. Explain why dark lines are still observed in the absorption spectrum.

markscheme_points.text: light is re-emitted in all directions

hints: Hint 1: When an atom absorbs a photon from the forward beam and then de-excites, does the new photon have to go forward toward the grating?
parts.proper_answer: Absorbed photons are re-emitted in all directions, so very little continues forward to the grating and dark lines are seen.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Follow The Photon Path**
An electron absorbs a photon of exactly the right energy and jumps up. Very quickly it falls back down and emits a photon of the same energy. So energy is conserved, nothing is lost overall.

Step 2: **Why It Still Looks Dark**
The key is direction. Absorption removes a photon from the narrow forward beam. Re-emission is spontaneous and random in direction - over a full $4\pi$ solid angle. Only a tiny fraction happens to go forward through the grating, so at that wavelength the forward intensity is much reduced and you see a dark line.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
Some of the energy levels of an electron in a hydrogen atom are illustrated in Fig. 10.1.

{{figure:figure_10_1}}

The dark lines in the absorption spectrum are the result of electron transitions between energy levels.

On Fig. 10.1, draw arrows to show the initial electron transitions between energy levels that could give rise to dark lines in the absorption spectrum.

markscheme_points.text: an arrow between $-3.40\text{ eV}$ and $-0.85\text{ eV}$

hints: Hint 1: For absorption, does the electron gain energy and move up to a higher level, or lose energy and move down?
Hint 2: Work out $\Delta E = E_{upper} - E_{lower}$ for pairs of levels and check which differences lie between $1.60\text{ eV}$ and $2.60\text{ eV}$.
parts.proper_answer: Draw upward arrows starting from $-3.40\text{ eV}$ to $-1.51\text{ eV}$ ($1.89\text{ eV}$) and from $-3.40\text{ eV}$ to $-0.85\text{ eV}$ ($2.55\text{ eV}$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Upwards For Absorption**
Dark lines in absorption mean photons are taken from the beam to excite electrons. The electron must gain energy, so on an energy-level diagram the arrow must point upwards from a lower to a higher level.

Step 2: **Match The Beam Energies**
Photon energy must equal the gap: $$\Delta E = E_{high} - E_{low}$$ The beam only has $1.60\text{ eV}$ to $2.60\text{ eV}$. Check from $-3.40\text{ eV}$: $$-1.51 - (-3.40) = 1.89\text{ eV}$$ which is allowed, and $$-0.85 - (-3.40) = 2.55\text{ eV}$$ which is also allowed. Other gaps, e.g. $-0.54 - (-3.40) = 2.86\text{ eV}$, are outside the range, and transitions from $-13.60\text{ eV}$ need about $10\text{ eV}$.

Step 3: **What To Draw**
So draw two upward arrows both starting at the $-3.40\text{ eV}$ level, one ending at $-1.51\text{ eV}$ and one ending at $-0.85\text{ eV}$. No downward arrows, because those would be emission.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Calculate the shortest wavelength of the light in the beam.
hints: Hint 1: For light, larger photon energy means larger or smaller wavelength? Decide which energy from the $1.60\text{ eV}$ to $2.60\text{ eV}$ range gives the shortest wavelength.
Hint 2: The photon formula uses SI units, so you will need to change electronvolts to joules using $1\text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$.
Hint 3: Link $E$, $h$, $c$ and $\lambda$ together and rearrange to make $\lambda$ the subject before substituting numbers.
parts.proper_answer: $E = hc/\lambda$ with $E = 2.60\text{ eV} = 4.16 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$ gives $\lambda = 4.8 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose The Right Energy**
Shortest wavelength means highest frequency and highest photon energy, because $$E = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$ So use the top of the range, $E = 2.60\text{ eV}$.

Step 2: **Convert To Joules**
$h$ and $c$ are in SI units, so $E$ must be in joules: $$E = 2.60 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J} = 4.16 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$$

Step 3: **Calculate Wavelength**
Rearrange $$E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$ to $$\lambda = \frac{hc}{E}$$ Then: $$\lambda = \frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34}) \times (3.00 \times 10^{8})}{4.16 \times 10^{-19}}$$ $$\lambda = 4.8 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}$$ This is in the visible blue-violet region, as expected.
